'''Michael Andrew Minovitch''' ({{circa}} 1936 - 16 September 2022)<ref name=BBC2012>{{cite news|author=Christopher Riley and Dallas Campbell |title=The maths that made Voyager possible |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/science-environment-20033940 |work=[[BBC News]] |date=October 23, 2012 |access-date=2014-10-14 }}</ref> was an American [[mathematician]] who developed [[gravity assist]] technique when he was a [[University of California, Los Angeles|UCLA]] [[Postgraduate education|graduate student]] and working summers at [[NASA]]'s [[Jet Propulsion Laboratory]].<ref>{{citation|last=Minovitch|first=Michael|title=An Alternative Method for Determination of Elliptic and Hyperbolic Trajectories|series=Jet Propulsion Laboratory Technical Memos|number=TM-312-118|date=July 11, 1961|url=http://www.gravityassist.com/Letters/LD-1.pdf#page=3}}</ref><ref>{{citation|last=Minovitch|first=Michael|title=A Method For Determining Interplanetary Free-Fall Reconnaissance Trajectories|series=Jet Propulsion Laboratory Technical Memos|number=TM-312-130|pages=38–44|date=August 23, 1961|url=http://www.gravityassist.com/Letters/LD-1.pdf#page=24}}</ref> He claimed that he invented the technique, even though multiple publications preceded his own. He later sued several people, including [[Richard Battin]] who published a paper on gravity assists in 1958, for stealing his ideas, but lost.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://heritageproject.caltech.edu/interviews-updates/gary-flandro |title=Gary Flandro (PHD '67), Aerospace Engineer |date=7 September 2022 }}</ref>

In 1961 Minovitch began using the fastest available computer at the time, the [[IBM 7090]], to find solutions of the [[three-body problem]]. He ran simulations and developed his own solution by 1962.<ref name=BBC2012 />

The first mission to use a gravity assist was [[Pioneer 10]], which increased its velocity from 52,000&nbsp;km/h to 132,000&nbsp;km/h as it passed by Jupiter in December, 1973.<ref>{{cite web | title=The Pioneer Missions|access-date=2015-01-29|date=March 26, 2007|website=www.nasa.gov|url=http://www.nasa.gov/centers/ames/missions/archive/pioneer.html}}</ref><ref>{{cite web | title=Slingshots and Space shots|publisher=[[American Mathematical Society]]|access-date=2015-01-29|author=Bill Casselman|url=http://www.ams.org/samplings/feature-column/fcarc-slingshot|author-link=Bill Casselman (mathematician)}}</ref>

Minovitch patented a vehicle for space travel under the patent title ''Magnetic propulsion system and operating method'', US Patent 6193194 B1.
